title: Leaders Usually Get the Team They Deserve
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership argues that team dysfunction is almost always a mirror of leadership behavior rather than bad luck or a weak team, because people read what leaders actually reward and tolerate far more reliably than what leaders claim to value. The piece works through matched examples: a leader who says they want candid feedback but punishes bad news trains the team to hide problems, while a leader who preaches accountability but avoids hard conversations trains the team to cut corners. The core mechanism identified is incentive-following behavior — teams optimize for whatever gets praised or recognized, so if busyness is rewarded over results, people perform busyness, and if loyalty outranks candor, people stop telling the truth. This cuts both ways, meaning consistent, disciplined leadership behavior builds a results-focused team just as surely as inconsistency erodes one. The piece stops short of claiming leaders control every variable, acknowledging markets shift and leaders sometimes inherit teams shaped by prior decisions, but insists that when the same problems recur under the same leadership, the most productive response is to look inward at hiring choices, promotion decisions, and what behaviors have been quietly tolerated before looking anywhere else.
points: Central claim: teams learn from what leaders do and reward, not from what leaders say they value, so recurring team dysfunction is usually traceable back to the leader's own tolerated behaviors and incentive structure rather than to the team itself.

Matched contrast examples make the mechanism concrete: claiming to value candid feedback while punishing bad news produces a team that hides problems; preaching accountability while avoiding hard conversations produces a team that cuts corners.

The piece frames team composition and culture as largely a product of leader decisions — who gets hired, who gets promoted, what behavior gets tolerated or let slide — rather than as an externally imposed given.

It explicitly limits the claim's scope, acknowledging leaders don't control every variable (market shifts, budget cuts, inherited teams), while still arguing that recurring problems under stable leadership warrant self-examination first.

The practical instruction offered is diagnostic: when frustrated by a team's short-term thinking or underperformance, a leader should ask what behavior and reward structure they are personally reinforcing before looking for other explanations.
quotes: Teams learn far more from what leaders do than from what they say.

A leader who claims to value candid feedback but punishes people for delivering bad news creates a team that hides problems. A leader who preaches accountability but never has hard conversations creates a team that cuts corners.
Teams optimize for whatever is actually rewarded and recognized, not for what leaders say is valued. If busyness gets praised more than results, people will look busy.
Far too many leaders scratch their heads, confused by a team that underperforms or doesn't meet their expectations. The problem is usually in the mirror.
The team is largely a product of the decisions leaders make — who they hire, who they promote, what behaviors they tolerate, and what they let slide.
This doesn't mean leaders control every variable. Markets shift, budgets shrink, and a leader sometimes inherits a team shaped by someone else's choices. No leader is omnipotent.
Accountability in teams begins with the leader who owns their part in the problem.
